title: Evaluation of State-of-the-Art Deep Learning Architectures for Aerodynamical Predictions
authors: Jan Scherz, Derrick Hines, Philipp Bekemeyer
abstract: Surrogate models are used to substitute classical numerical solvers in engineering applications where the computational cost of the latter becomes infeasible. For instance, in aerodynamics such models offer cost-effective alternatives to computational fluid dynamics in problems such as shape optimization and load analysis, which oftentimes require high-fidelity simulations for a multitude of different parameter combinations. A specific class of deep learning-based surrogate models termed operator learning models directly approximates the solution operators to the partial differential equations underlying the physical phenomenon, thereby learning to replicate solutions to entire families of problems. However, while nowadays numerous architectures of this type get published, corresponding benchmark studies remain scarce. In this article, we advance the study of AI-based surrogate methods by thoroughly benchmarking four state-of-the-art operator learning models on their aptitude for applications in aerospace engineering. In two experiments, we assess the models' capabilities of predicting the surface pressure distribution on two-dimensional airfoil shapes of varying complexity and on an industrial-scale three-dimensional aircraft configuration. Thereby, we evaluate the models' abilities to fulfill frequent requirements in aerodynamics such as capturing discontinuities (shocks) in the solutions, scalability towards excessive amounts of mesh points and handling of data scarcity. Accompanied by a careful analysis, our findings drive forward the field of AI-based surrogate modeling by providing detailed insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the individual architectures, thus allowing to identify priorities for future developments. In particular the Bi-Stride Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network and Transolver(++) are highlighted as promising surrogate models for aerodynamical applications.

infographic.key_insight: The paper benchmarks four operator-learning surrogates for aerodynamics and finds that Bi-Stride Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network and Transolver(++) are the most promising for predicting pressure fields on airfoils and aircraft.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models could reduce CFD cost for design optimization and load analysis by approximating pressure distributions across many geometries and flow conditions.
method: Benchmarked 4 state-of-the-art operator learning architectures
Tested 2D airfoils of varying complexity and a 3D industrial aircraft configuration
Assessed shock capture, scalability to large meshes, and performance under data scarcity
infographic.evidence_signal: The evaluation spans two experiments on aerodynamic pressure prediction, focusing on surface pressure distributions and comparing model behavior across discontinuities, mesh size, and limited training data.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on architecture and problem setting, so these surrogates still need careful validation before deployment on new geometries or flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluation of State-of-the-Art Deep Learning Architectures for Aerodynamical Predictions

title: Generating synthetic evolution of turbulent flames with an experimental data-based spatiotemporal diffusion model
authors: Amrit Tarur, Shivam Barwey
abstract: In this study, a conditional diffusion model -- a class of generative machine learning models -- is developed to generate synthetic, experimental data-based trajectories of turbulent flames. Generated experimental data corresponds to simultaneous field measurements, namely OH planar laser-induced fluorescence (OH-PLIF) fields and multi-component particle image velocimetry (PIV) fields, for attached and detached flame states in a swirl combustor configuration. This is done using an x-prediction flow matching framework combined with a pixel-based spatiotemporal transformer, which is capable of generating entire spatiotemporal slabs containing synthetic flame evolution at inference time, conditioned on the flame regime. Using this framework, synthetic flames were found to preserve key flame features and statistical consistency across space and time, particularly at the large scales -- deviations at high temporal frequencies and small spatial length scales were found to depend on the time-span of the generated space-time slabs. An extrapolation task of transition synthesis is also conducted, in which the conditional diffusion model is used to synthesize spatiotemporally coherent flame transitions (flame liftoff and reattachment) unseen by the model during training. This was accomplished using a model for the denoising transition velocity that relies on time-varying linear combinations of attached and detached denoising velocities, leading to an approach that (a) allows for control of the generated transition directions and timescales, and (b) retains sample-to-sample variability in the generated transitions in the process. Overall, this study provides a promising pathway for the utilization of experimental data-based generative models as a new means of data exploration in data-sparse environments, complementing both experiments and computational fluid dynamics-based approaches.

infographic.key_insight: A conditional diffusion model can generate realistic synthetic turbulent-flame evolution from experimental OH-PLIF and PIV data, including unseen transition events like liftoff and reattachment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a data-driven tool to augment scarce flame measurements and support combustion analysis, regime exploration, and model validation beyond traditional experiments and CFD.
method: Uses an x-prediction flow matching diffusion framework.
Combines a pixel-based spatiotemporal transformer with regime conditioning.
Synthesizes full space-time slabs and a transition-velocity model for controlled flame-state changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The generated flames preserved key features and statistical consistency across space and time, especially at large scales, while transition synthesis produced spatiotemporally coherent liftoff and reattachment not seen during training.
infographic.watch_item: High-frequency temporal details and small-scale spatial structures can deviate from real data, and performance depends on the generated slab time span.
infographic.paper_title: Generating synthetic evolution of turbulent flames with an experimental data-based spatiotemporal diffusion model

title: Turbulent boundary layers altered by passively rotating discs
authors: Max W. Knoop, Pierre Ricco
abstract: Turbulent boundary layers characterised by friction Reynolds numbers in the range $Re_τ = 880 - 1460$ and flowing over flush-mounted passively rotating discs are investigated in a wind tunnel with the purpose of reducing the skin-friction drag. The test surface is composed of thirty-two rotating discs arranged in a staggered configuration and supported by bearings mounted in cylindrical cavities. As the discs are half covered by thin rigid plates, a steady rotation of the discs is sustained via the asymmetric distribution of the wall-shear stress exerted by the wall turbulence on the exposed halves of the discs. Direct force measurements reveal that the drag increases with respect to a flat-plate case because of the flow interaction with the disc housings and the covering plates. The effect of the disc motion is isolated and a 3\% drag reduction is measured with respect to the flow over stationary discs. The skin-friction identity by \cite{Elnahhas_Johnson_2022} (\emph{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol. 940, 2022), extended herein to include the disc-flow effects, is utilised for the first time to analyse experimental data. This direct slip effect, quantified by using the measured disc angular velocities in the Elnahhas-Johnson identity, is negligible. Measurements obtained by particle image velocimetry disclose that a roughness mean-flow effect occurs between adjacent discs because of the clearance gaps around the discs and that a downwash secondary flow exists near the covering plates, analogous to flows over streamwise-elongated rectangular roughness elements. This downwash velocity is streamwise modulated because of the spanwise disc motion and alters the wall-normal transport term in the Elnahhas-Johnson identity, thus reducing the drag locally.

infographic.key_insight: Passively rotating, flush-mounted discs can slightly reduce turbulent boundary-layer skin friction, but the benefit is small and only emerges after accounting for geometry-induced drag penalties and local flow changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study informs low-power surface-texturing strategies for drag management in wall-bounded turbulence, especially where passive motion can be induced by the flow itself.
method: Wind-tunnel experiments on turbulent boundary layers with $Re_\tau=880$–1460 over 32 staggered rotating discs
Direct force measurements to separate total drag, disc-motion effects, and stationary-disc baseline
Particle image velocimetry plus the extended Elnahhas-Johnson skin-friction identity to diagnose mean-flow and slip contributions
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments showed the full disc housing/cover system increased drag relative to a flat plate, while isolating disc motion revealed a 3% drag reduction versus stationary discs, with the direct slip effect found to be negligible.
infographic.watch_item: The practical benefit is constrained by added drag from cavities and cover plates, so geometry details and gap-flow interactions must be controlled carefully before any implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Turbulent boundary layers altered by passively rotating discs

title: Drawing with water waves
authors: Taiga Kanehira, James Steer, Laura-Beth Jordan, Shaun Fraser, Thomas Davey, Hidemi Mutsuda
abstract: The deterministic reproduction of complex 3D wave fields remains a significant challenge in ocean engineering. This study proposes a novel methodology for drawing arbitrary 2D curves and 3D volumetric shapes on a water surface using transient multi-directional focused waves. To overcome the limitations of conventional discrete-point focusing methods, our framework integrates Bézier curve parametrisation, equal arc-length sampling, and an Iterative Amplitude Correction (IAC) algorithm. This effectively mitigates wave height overshoot and enables precise spatial superposition of spectral components. The method's effectiveness was validated through linear wave theory and Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, successfully reproducing 2D characters and a 3D human face. Physical experiments in the FloWave circular wave basin further demonstrated target shape generation, such as a 2D star and 3D pyramid. Although further integration of nonlinear wave theories is necessary for high-amplitude accuracy, this technique establishes a deterministic methodology for creating arbitrary 2D and 3D surface geometries. It represents a significant advantage in wave field control for ocean engineering applications.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a deterministic way to “draw” arbitrary 2D curves and 3D shapes on water by combining focused transient waves with curve-based sampling and amplitude correction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more precise wave-field shaping for ocean engineering, with potential uses in wave control, experimental testing, and programmable surface pattern generation.
method: Parameterize target shapes with Bézier curves
Sample the curve at equal arc length to place wave foci
Use Iterative Amplitude Correction (IAC) to reduce overshoot and improve superposition
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach was validated with linear wave theory, SPH simulations, and physical FloWave basin experiments that reproduced 2D and 3D target shapes such as a star and pyramid.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy may degrade for larger-amplitude waves because nonlinear wave effects are not yet fully incorporated.
infographic.paper_title: Drawing with water waves

title: Condition for $1/f$ noise to occur along with an example for a diffusion equation
authors: H. Mouri
abstract: While $1/f$ noise is ubiquitous and has been found in various systems, its physics remains uncertain. From an analytical study of an ordinary diffusion equation, we find an additional example of the $1/f$ noise. The formula for this example, together with existing knowledge about scaling in fluid turbulence, implies a necessary and sufficient condition for the occurrence of any stationary $1/f$ noise. That is, the noise needs to be characterized by two constant frequencies of $f_{\rm low} \ll f_{\rm high}$. For a frequency range from $f = f_{\rm low}$ to $f_{\rm high}$, it is further needed that, except for the mean amplitude of the noise, there is no other constant parameter. Then, at $f_{\rm low} \ll f \ll f_{\rm high}$, the noise scales asymptotically as $1/f$. Being statistical and simple, our condition applies to any system and hence explains the ubiquity of the $1/f$ noise. It is also applicable to some systems with noise of $α\ne 1.0$ for $1/f^α$, via intermittency analogous to that of the turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: A stationary 1/f spectrum emerges when a system is described by two separated frequency scales (flowing from f_low to f_high) and no other constant parameter besides the mean amplitude, making 1/f noise a generic asymptotic outcome.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a simple, system-agnostic criterion for identifying or designing components and models that may exhibit 1/f-type fluctuations, including turbulence-like intermittent regimes.
method: Analytical study of the ordinary diffusion equation
Combined the derived spectrum with known scaling results from fluid turbulence
Used the result to infer a necessary and sufficient condition for stationary 1/f noise
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical derivation and comparison with established turbulence scaling; no new experimental or numerical dataset is mentioned.
infographic.watch_item: The condition is stated for stationary noise over a clear frequency band, so real systems with extra parameters, finite-size effects, or nonstationarity may deviate from ideal 1/f behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Condition for $1/f$ noise to occur along with an example for a diffusion equation

title: Coherence as Thermodynamic Organization: Toward a Non-Equilibrium Turbulence Theory
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Since the foundational studies in the late nineteenth century, fluid turbulence has stood as a profound, unsolved challenge in classical physics. Much of this enduring difficulty stems from non-equilibrium turbulence, where the lack of a unifying physical framework for macroscopic coherent structures has hampered predictive flow modeling. Here, we establish a foundational bridge between non-equilibrium statistical physics and turbulent coherent structures through the renormalized Navier-Stokes equations. We demonstrate that all forms of turbulent coherence are fundamentally universal thermodynamic responses mandated by macroscopic energy throughput imbalances. Depending on topological access to bifurcations, these formations manifest either as transient adjustments (analogous to Kubo's near-equilibrium fluctuations) or as autonomous, transformative states (mirroring Prigogine's far-from-equilibrium dissipative structures). By introducing a computable, effective thermodynamic order parameter ($Π$), this paradigm establishes a rigorous foundation for non-equilibrium theory, enabling unequivocal identification of necessary flow resolution in continuously driven, dissipative continuum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent coherent structures are framed as universal thermodynamic responses to energy-throughput imbalance, with a computable order parameter (Π) distinguishing transient fluctuations from autonomous dissipative states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help determine what flow features must be resolved in simulations and experiments, improving predictive modeling of continuously driven turbulent systems.
method: Recast turbulent coherence through renormalized Navier–Stokes equations.
Link non-equilibrium fluid behavior to thermodynamic concepts from Kubo and Prigogine.
Introduce an effective thermodynamic order parameter (Π) for identifying coherent structure and required resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theory/framework and claims a computable order parameter, but does not report specific datasets, benchmarks, or numerical validation results.
infographic.watch_item: The order parameter and coherence classification may be theoretically powerful, but practical robustness will depend on how Π is computed and validated across diverse turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Coherence as Thermodynamic Organization: Toward a Non-Equilibrium Turbulence Theory

title: NeuroForge: A Self-Correcting, Geometry-Native Neural CFD Engine with Calibrated Physics-Residual Trust
authors: Ali Jabbary, Kasra Ghanavati
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) predict steady flow fields orders of magnitude faster than classical solvers, but emit a single field with no built-in way to know whether to trust it -- especially out of distribution. We close the loop with the governing physics: we compute the discretised steady-RANS residual of the prediction and ask what jobs it can do. Our central finding is a two-way dissociation: the physics residual is a reliable, backbone-robust trust signal (it tells you where the prediction is wrong) but a poor correction objective (it does not tell you how to fix it). As a trust signal, the residual's per-case rank correlation with field error is consistently positive across three architecturally distinct backbones (Transolver 0.625+-0.019; grid Geo-FNO ~0.40, lifted to 0.83 by a learned corrector; MeshGraphNet 0.851+-0.058) and generalizes to a second dataset and flow regime (DeepCFD laminar bluff bodies, rho=0.77+-0.12). A split-conformal layer attains target coverage (0.902+-0.008 at the 0.90 target) and, paired with a deep-ensemble sigma, yields an input-adaptive band (ECE 0.074). As a correction objective or acceptance gate the residual fails: iteration sweeps raise the PDE residual while lowering field error. Alongside the trust layer we deploy a supervised deep-equilibrium corrector trained toward ground truth that reduces volume-field MSE on all three seeds (mse_u -9%, mse_v -21%, mse_p -25%) on the SOTA backbone; a controlled ablation zeroing the corrector's residual input matches it, so the gain is attributable to the learned correction, not residual-conditioning. We report caveats plainly: correction quality is backbone-dependent, and the coverage guarantee holds under exchangeability. The contribution is a self-auditing trust layer, the residual's two roles, and the learned self-correction it accompanies.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that steady-RANS residuals are a strong, backbone-robust signal for detecting CFD prediction errors, but they are weak as a direct correction target.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster CFD surrogates to be paired with calibrated uncertainty and self-correction, improving trustworthiness for design and screening workflows.
method: Compute the discretized steady-RANS residual of surrogate flow predictions as a trust indicator.
Use split-conformal calibration, combined with deep-ensemble uncertainty, to produce adaptive confidence bands.
Train a supervised deep-equilibrium corrector to improve predicted fields toward ground truth.
infographic.evidence_signal: Residual-error rank correlation is consistently positive across Transolver, Geo-FNO, and MeshGraphNet, generalizes to DeepCFD, and conformal coverage reaches 0.902 at a 0.90 target.
infographic.watch_item: The correction performance depends on the backbone, and the coverage guarantee only holds under exchangeability assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: NeuroForge: A Self-Correcting, Geometry-Native Neural CFD Engine with Calibrated Physics-Residual Trust

title: Gradient-free learning of a closed-loop wall controller for turbulent drag reduction
authors: Giorgio Maria Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez Cuadrado, Alfredo Pinelli
abstract: Closed-loop wall control learnt by multi-agent reinforcement learning can lower skin-friction drag in turbulent channels, but these gradient-based policies are trained on small periodic boxes and exhibit reduced performance when carried over to a larger domain. We recently showed that such policies are also prone to saturated bang-bang actuations that collapse into standing streamwise waves whose scale is set by the computational box rather than by the near-wall cycle, and proposed architectural fixes that avoid these degeneracies. Here, we employ Evolution Strategy (ES) to optimise a recurrent closed-loop controller directly on a large turbulent channel at $\mathit{Re}_τ\simeq180$, evaluating policy performance over full flow episodes using an energy-aware criterion and processing candidate policies in parallel. To our knowledge, this is the first application of an evolution strategy to the control of a turbulent flow. The ES controller reduces the skin friction by about $26\%$, exceeding the gradient-based multi-agent controller of Cavallazzi et al. (2026), GRU-MARL, trained on a minimal box ($17\%$), and marginally exceeding classic opposition control (OC, $22\%$). A wall-normal decomposition of the friction, Reynolds-stress profiles and anisotropy invariants show that the ES and opposition-controlled flows follow separate trajectories through the buffer layer, reaching comparable drag reduction by different reorganisations of the near-wall turbulence. In particular, the ES actuation correlates predominantly with the streamwise velocity fluctuations rather than with the wall-normal velocity that classical OC targets.

infographic.key_insight: Evolution Strategy trained directly on a large turbulent channel learns a recurrent wall controller that avoids small-box degeneracies and cuts skin-friction drag by about 26%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests gradient-free closed-loop control can scale better than prior MARL policies for practical turbulent drag-reduction designs in larger domains.
method: Optimize a recurrent controller with Evolution Strategy instead of backpropagation.
Evaluate candidate policies over full flow episodes using an energy-aware objective.
Train and test directly in a large channel at Re_tau ≃ 180 with parallel policy evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The ES controller reduced drag by about 26%, outperforming GRU-MARL trained on a minimal box (17%) and slightly exceeding classic opposition control (22%).
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on full-episode, large-domain evaluation, so controllers trained in smaller periodic boxes may not transfer reliably and can still be sensitive to actuation degeneracies.
infographic.paper_title: Gradient-free learning of a closed-loop wall controller for turbulent drag reduction

title: A multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network for fluid dynamics prediction in complex geometries
authors: Li Xiao, Tianyu Li, Yiye Zou, Mingjie Zhang, Xiaogangd Deng
abstract: Industrial design in fields such as vehicle and aerospace engineering often relies on large-scale numerical simulations to evaluate fluid dynamics performance, which can incur substantial computational costs. Deep neural networks have shown promise in improving simulation efficiency, especially graph neural networks (GNNs), which demonstrate great potential due to their flexibility with unstructured data. However, GNNs face challenges when dealing with tasks involving complex geometries and large-scale meshes. In this paper, we propose the Multi-scale Feature Enhanced Graph Neural Network (ME-GNN) to tackle these challenges. ME-GNN employs a graph neural network with a two-step message-passing mechanism to capture detailed local features effectively. Additionally, it integrates an Attention U-Net with uniform grid discretization, enabling the extraction of both fine and coarse features. The model also utilizes K-hop sampling to construct subgraphs, facilitating efficient training on large datasets while preserving detailed local features. We evaluated ME-GNN on three benchmark datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results: a relative L2 error of 0.0196 for the velocity field and 0.0556 for the surface pressure on ShapeNet-Car, a normalized mean squared error of 0.0033 for the flow field on AirfRANS, and a relative L2 error of 0.1416 for the surface pressure on DrivAerNet.

infographic.key_insight: ME-GNN combines local graph message passing, multi-scale grid features, and subgraph sampling to improve fluid-field prediction in complex geometries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can reduce reliance on expensive CFD simulations for automotive and aerospace design workflows on large, irregular meshes.
method: Two-step GNN message passing for detailed local feature aggregation
Attention U-Net on uniform grids to capture fine and coarse flow structures
K-hop subgraph sampling to train efficiently on large-scale meshes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art benchmark performance, including 0.0196 velocity-field relative L2 error on ShapeNet-Car and 0.0033 normalized MSE on AirfRANS.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful subgraph sampling and grid-to-graph feature alignment, which could be challenging on highly irregular industrial meshes.
infographic.paper_title: A multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network for fluid dynamics prediction in complex geometries

title: Mixing and sharpening at the interface of a two-layer fluid forced by random jets
authors: Noé Clavier, Hugo Pradel, Romain Volk, Mickaël Bourgoin, Yvan Dossmann
abstract: Understanding mixing at density interfaces is essential for predicting transport in stratified environmental flows. Laboratory studies have mostly relied on steady, spatially uniform forcing, whereas turbulence in nature is intermittent and heterogeneous. Here, we present experiments on a two-layer salt-stratified fluid forced by random turbulent bursts generated with a randomly actuated synthetic jet array (RASJA). Density fields are recorded with the light attenuation technique, allowing us to resolve the interface evolution. We measure that the upward velocity of the interface decreases with the density jump, in agreement with the power-law found in previous oscillating-grid studies. At large density differences, the interface sharpens during mixing, contrary to the smaller density jump case. Background potential energy analysis demonstrates irreversible mixing in both cases, with comparable energy changes. These results extend classical laboratory observations to a more isotropic forcing, offering new insights into the dynamics of mixing in geophysical settings.

infographic.key_insight: Random intermittent jet forcing can drive mixing at a salt-stratified interface, and at large density jumps the interface can sharpen even while irreversible mixing still occurs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results inform how heterogeneous, bursty forcing may transport and restructure stratified fluids in environmental and industrial mixing systems.
method: Two-layer salt-stratified fluid experiment forced by a randomly actuated synthetic jet array (RASJA).
Interface evolution measured with light attenuation to resolve density-field changes.
Compared interface motion and sharpening across different density jumps and linked changes to background potential energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements show interface upward velocity decreases as the density jump increases, and background potential energy indicates irreversible mixing in both regimes.
infographic.watch_item: The findings come from laboratory two-layer conditions, so direct scaling to strongly three-dimensional or field-scale stratified flows may require caution.
infographic.paper_title: Mixing and sharpening at the interface of a two-layer fluid forced by random jets

title: Dynamics of a microroller under confinement
authors: Han Gao, Nan Xie, Zaiyi Shen, Xiaoping Hu, Shiyuan Hu, Ye Xu
abstract: Rotating particles can translate when placed near a surface, forming microrollers with a wide range of biomedical and microfluidic applications. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of microrollers in confined microchannels with different geometries by combining experiments, numerical simulations, and scaling analysis. In constricted channels, we find that the translational velocity of a microroller decreases as it approaches the constricted region. In both rectangular and cylindrical channels, velocity reversal occurs as the characteristic channel width decreases. Using the force-free condition for free translation, we develop a systematic scaling framework that can be generalized to different channel geometries. The scaling analysis yields functional dependences of the translational velocity on the degree of confinement, which agree well with both experiments and simulations. Importantly, we demonstrate that the viscous stress generated by the far-field rotlet flow governs the observed velocity reduction and reversal, while the translational resistance resulting from the near-field shear flow suppresses translation under tight confinement. The distinct roles of these flow components revealed by our analysis may provide practical guidance for controlling microroller dynamics in confined fluid environments.

infographic.key_insight: Microroller speed drops as confinement increases, and in sufficiently narrow channels the motion can reverse direction because far-field rotlet stresses and near-field shear resistance compete.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scaling framework provides a geometry-aware way to predict and control microroller transport in microfluidic and biomedical devices under confined flow conditions.
method: Experiments in constricted, rectangular, and cylindrical microchannels
Numerical simulations of microroller translation under varying confinement
Scaling analysis using a force-free translation condition across geometries
infographic.evidence_signal: The proposed scaling laws for translational velocity match the experimental and simulation results across multiple channel geometries and confinement levels.
infographic.watch_item: The velocity reversal depends strongly on channel geometry and tight confinement, so designs may need geometry-specific calibration rather than a single universal threshold.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamics of a microroller under confinement

title: Numerical Simulation of Turbulent Concentric Annular Pipe Flow using One-Dimensional Turbulence (ODT): Part 2: Heat Transfer
authors: Pei-Yun Tsai, Heiko Schmidt, Marten Klein
abstract: Turbulent concentric coaxial (annular) pipe flow with passive heat transfer is theoretically analyzed and numerically modeled in an extended parametric range using the stochastic one-dimensional turbulence (ODT) model. ODT provides predictive capabilities by fully resolving viscous, conductive, and turbulent advective transport processes along a representative radial coordinate within a dimensionally reduced and stochastic model formulation. Using a fixed model calibration for moderate and low Prandtl numbers, $Pr=0.71$ and $0.025$, effects of radius ratio, $η=R_{\rm i}/R_{\rm o}$ are investigated up to a highly turbulent flow regime. The analytical expression of the inner wall boundary layer yields a logarithmic law of the wall for the passive temperature. These results suggest that a conventional linear expression is inadequate for representing near-wall low-order statistics in the radial gap, in particular at the cylindrical inner wall. Additionally, the log-law region falls short if curvature and finite Reynolds number effects are not considered. Analytical boundary layer profiles fitting numerical predictions form the basis for heat transfer scaling relations. Heat transfer scalings are parameterized by a Nusselt correlation, which is extended to account for radius ratio effects. The findings demonstrate that the radius ratio has a significant impact on the thermal statistics over the two curved walls and should be considered even at high Reynolds numbers and low Prandtl numbers.

infographic.key_insight: ODT predicts that heat transfer in turbulent concentric annular pipe flow is strongly affected by radius ratio, with near-wall temperature following a logarithmic rather than linear law, especially near the inner curved wall.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Radius-ratio-dependent Nusselt correlations and wall-scaling laws can improve thermal design of annular ducts, coaxial pipes, and similar curved-wall cooling/heating systems.
method: Stochastic one-dimensional turbulence (ODT) resolves viscous, conductive, and turbulent advective transport along a representative radial coordinate.
Parametric study spans radius ratio, curvature, Reynolds number, and two Prandtl numbers (0.71 and 0.025).
Boundary-layer analysis is used to derive wall-temperature laws and heat-transfer scaling relations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was evaluated against analytical boundary-layer expressions and numerical predictions across an extended parametric range, showing consistent radius-ratio effects and the need for log-law-based wall fits.
infographic.watch_item: A conventional linear near-wall temperature profile can be misleading in curved annular flows, so calibration and scaling should account for curvature and finite-Re effects.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Simulation of Turbulent Concentric Annular Pipe Flow using One-Dimensional Turbulence (ODT): Part 2: Heat Transfer

title: Metamorphosis of transition between states of limit cycle oscillations in aeroacoustic system
authors: Siddharth Kancharlapalli, Beeraiah Thonti, Sivakumar Sudarshanan, Ramesh S. Bhavi, R. I. Sujith
abstract: Dynamical systems undergoing transition to oscillatory state exhibit change in the nature of the transition from supercritical to subcritical Hopf bifurcation or vice versa upon variation of a secondary parameter. This phenomenon is referred to as change of criticality. Many real-world systems undergo transition to oscillatory state that do not fit in the framework of Hopf bifurcation, and hence the change of criticality. We perform experiments on a ducted turbulent aeroacoustic flow constrained by two orifices separated at a distance apart. We vary the Reynolds number (Re), a bifurcation parameter causing a transition between various limit cycles. We change the distance between the orifices as the secondary parameter. We discover that turbulent aeroacoustic flows exhibit a metamorphosis of the transition from continuous to abrupt through a canard explosion, a bifurcation unique for its continuous yet rapid nature. We observe two distinct abrupt bifurcations, differing in their dynamical states associated with the transition. Understanding this metamorphosis from continuous to abrupt aids in developing low-cost control and preventive strategies for systems undergoing a route to oscillatory instabilities.

infographic.key_insight: In a ducted turbulent aeroacoustic flow, changing the spacing between two orifices can metamorphose the onset of limit-cycle oscillations from continuous to abrupt, with a canard explosion mediating the transition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reveals a controllable route to oscillatory instability in aeroacoustic systems, supporting low-cost design and mitigation strategies for noise and instability control.
method: Conducted experiments on ducted turbulent flow with two orifices separated by varying distances.
Varied Reynolds number as the bifurcation parameter driving transitions between limit cycles.
Used the orifice spacing as a secondary parameter to observe changes in transition criticality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental observation of two distinct abrupt bifurcations, including a continuous-to-abrupt metamorphosis through a canard explosion.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are based on a specific ducted aeroacoustic configuration, so the transition types and control implications may not generalize without validation in other geometries and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Metamorphosis of transition between states of limit cycle oscillations in aeroacoustic system

title: Data driven non-equilibrium moist phase exchanges for atmospheric convection within a discontinuous Galerkin model of the compressible Euler equations
authors: David Lee, Kieran Ricardo, Junwei Lyu
abstract: A neural network is trained to learn the mass exchanges between vapour, liquid and ice phases in atmospheric convection. The network is trained on convection resolving output from a regional configuration of the LFRic model with a multi-moment microphysics parameterisation (CASIM). The loss function for learning these phase exchanges is formulated under the assumptions of thermal and mechanical equilibrium (same temperature and pressure for all phases), and mechanical dis-equilibrium (different Gibbs free energies for all phases). The network outputs determine the exchanges of vapour, liquid and ice so as to conserve mass, and the resulting change in entropy is determined from the network outputs so as to conserve energy. The neural network is implemented in a thermodynamically consistent manner within a 2D vertical slice discontinuous Galerkin model of a moist, non-hydrostatic atmosphere in order to simulate the formation of three-phase clouds for convection at sub-km resolution. The results are compared to those from a physics based representation of three-phase moist processes at thermodynamic equilibrium.

infographic.key_insight: A thermodynamically constrained neural network can learn phase-change rates between vapour, liquid, and ice and embed them into a discontinuous Galerkin atmospheric model while conserving mass and energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a surrogate microphysics option for sub-kilometre convection simulations that could reduce reliance on expensive physics-based moist-process parameterisations.
method: Trained on convection-resolving output from a regional LFRic model using the CASIM microphysics scheme.
Network predicts mass exchanges among vapour, liquid, and ice under thermal/mechanical equilibrium assumptions.
Entropy change is derived from the learned exchanges to enforce energy consistency in the DG moist atmosphere model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is evaluated by running a 2D vertical-slice non-hydrostatic DG atmosphere simulation and comparing three-phase cloud formation against a physics-based equilibrium moist-process representation.
infographic.watch_item: Because the surrogate is trained on a specific regional configuration and equilibrium assumptions, its robustness outside the training regime and in strongly non-equilibrium conditions may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Data driven non-equilibrium moist phase exchanges for atmospheric convection within a discontinuous Galerkin model of the compressible Euler equations

title: Heuristic Learning for Active Flow Control Using Coding Agents
authors: Paul Garnier, Jonathan Viquerat, Elie Hachem
abstract: Active flow control involves nonlinear dynamics, partial observations, and computationally expensive simulations, making controller design particularly challenging. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a powerful framework for such problems, but its success typically relies on large numbers of simulator interactions and produces neural-network policies whose decision process often remains difficult to interpret. In this work, we investigate a different paradigm: instead of optimizing neural-network parameters, we use modern coding agents to search directly for explicit executable feedback laws. We introduce a constrained heuristic-learning protocol in which an agent iteratively proposes, evaluates, and revises controller implementations while interacting exclusively through the public benchmark interface. The proposed framework is evaluated on 13 active flow-control benchmarks spanning one, two, and three-dimensional problems and compared against the strongest available DRL baselines under identical simulation budgets. The discovered heuristic controllers match or outperform the best DRL policy in 10 of the 13 environments while remaining compact, interpretable, and directly inspectable. Beyond aggregate performance, the resulting controllers reveal physically meaningful feedback mechanisms, transfer successfully across more challenging configurations, and remain competitive under varying Reynolds and Rayleigh numbers, actuator counts, and observation sparsity. These results suggest that heuristic learning through coding agents constitutes a credible and complementary alternative to conventional reinforcement learning, combining competitive performance with physically interpretable controller representations. Prompts and source code are available at https://github.com/DonsetPG/fluid-heuristic-learning.

infographic.key_insight: Coding agents can directly search for explicit, interpretable feedback laws for active flow control and achieve DRL-level or better performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical alternative to black-box reinforcement learning for flow-control systems where simulator cost, partial observability, and interpretability matter.
method: Use a constrained heuristic-learning protocol with a coding agent proposing executable controllers.
Evaluate and revise controller code only through the public benchmark interface.
Compare learned heuristics against strong DRL baselines under identical simulation budgets across 13 benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 13 active flow-control benchmarks in 1D, 2D, and 3D, the discovered controllers matched or outperformed the best DRL policy in 10 environments under the same simulation budget.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the benchmark interface and careful constraint design, so results may not transfer unchanged to closed or more complex real-world control setups.
infographic.paper_title: Heuristic Learning for Active Flow Control Using Coding Agents

title: Physics informed wavelet Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics
authors: Chao Wang, Shilong Li, Yunpeng Wang, Tianbai Xiao, Zelong Yuan, Chenyue Xie
abstract: Multiscale fluid flows often contain localized flow structures, such as viscous shock layers, wet-dry fronts, steady viscous wakes, decaying vortical structures, and vortex-shedding patterns, whose accurate prediction requires the simultaneous preservation of global conservation trends and small-scale gradients. This study examines these flow-physics requirements through a physics-informed wavelet-Fourier (PIWF) representation for multiscale fluid dynamics. Instead of relying on a single monolithic neural approximator, the formulation separates two complementary components of the flow field within a physics-informed neural representation: long-range coherent modes through a Fourier-basis branch and localized steep-gradient or vortical features through a compactly supported wavelet branch. The outputs are fused with a residual multilayer perceptron using channel attention, and the governing equations, initial conditions, and boundary conditions are imposed directly through the physics-informed loss. The model is assessed on five canonical fluid-dynamics problems: Burgers' equation, the shallow water equations, Kovasznay flow, Taylor--Green vortex flow, and two-dimensional cylinder wake flow. The results show that PIWF improves the resolution of shock-like gradients, wet--dry interfaces, steady wake fields, decaying vortical structures, vorticity extrema, and broadband wake spectra relative to standard physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks. These findings indicate that a wavelet-Fourier physics-informed representation can provide a useful route for analyzing multiscale flow phenomena when high-fidelity interior reference data are limited or unavailable.

infographic.key_insight: PIWF splits multiscale flow learning into Fourier modes for global coherence and wavelets for localized sharp features, then enforces physics through the loss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical surrogate for fluid problems with shocks, fronts, wakes, and vortices when dense interior measurements are unavailable.
method: Fourier branch models long-range coherent structures.
Wavelet branch captures compact, steep-gradient and vortical features.
Residual MLP with channel attention fuses both branches under physics-informed constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on five canonical flow problems—Burgers, shallow water, Kovasznay flow, Taylor–Green vortex, and 2D cylinder wake—and reported better capture of gradients, interfaces, wakes, vortices, and spectra than PINNs and PI-KANs.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful balancing of Fourier and wavelet branches plus the physics-loss terms, which can be sensitive for complex geometries or noisy boundary data.
infographic.paper_title: Physics informed wavelet Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics

title: Emergent coordination and propulsion of a model spherical ciliate
authors: Hang Su, Timothy A Westwood, Eric E Keaveny
abstract: A longstanding challenge in biofluid dynamics research is a mechanistic understanding of the coordinated movement of motile cilia and its resulting ability to facilitate fluid transport. In this study, we develop numerical techniques to simultaneously compute the emergent coordination of and propulsion by filamentous model cilia covering the surface of a sphere. To accomplish this, we develop what we refer to as the filament oscillator model, in which each cilium has two dynamic degrees of freedom: a phase variable that maps to a specific shape in a prescribed sequence, and an angle that describes the overall orientation of the sequence. By varying a parameter related to cilium stiffness, we show that there is bistability between symplectic-like and diaplectic metachronal waves, provided that the stiffness is sufficiently low. Above the critical stiffness, only diaplectic waves emerge. Further, we analyse the propulsive capabilities and flow fields of the two emergent states, showing that diaplectic waves provide more efficient propulsion due to their shorter wavelengths. In addition, we examine how introducing beat-plane tilt leads to ciliate rotation while maintaining nearly identical emergent states and comparable swimming speeds.

infographic.key_insight: A filament oscillator model shows that coordinated ciliary waves can spontaneously switch between symplectic-like and diaplectic metachronal patterns, with stiffness controlling which state emerges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results inform how surface-bound active filaments should be tuned to maximize propulsion and control flow in synthetic microswimmers and bioinspired pumping systems.
method: Model each cilium with two degrees of freedom: phase along a prescribed beat sequence and overall orientation angle.
Simulate a spherical carpet of filamentous cilia to capture emergent coordination and propulsion simultaneously.
Sweep cilium stiffness and beat-plane tilt to test wave selection, swimming speed, flow structure, and rotation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical evaluation showing bistability at low stiffness, only diaplectic waves above a critical stiffness, and higher propulsive efficiency for diaplectic waves due to shorter wavelengths.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions come from a model system on a sphere, so real ciliary carpets may differ in geometry, hydrodynamic coupling, and biological variability.
infographic.paper_title: Emergent coordination and propulsion of a model spherical ciliate

title: Feature-based manifold model of actuated wakes
authors: Alicia Rodríguez-Asensio, Guy Y. Cornejo Maceda, Bernd R. Noack, Stefano Discetti, Andrea Ianiro
abstract: We propose a feature-based reduced-order model to predict the transient dynamics of bluff-body wakes under arbitrary time-varying actuation. Starting point is a control-oriented POD Galerkin modeling which is challenged by incorporating time-varying actuations as a free input. Our model includes three key enablers. First, POD modes are replaced by a more accurate feature-based manifold of same dimension. Second, a state space is distilled from dynamic features which encapsulate time-varying coherent structures. Third, this state space is augmented for the transient actuation response. Thus, a simple analytical manifold dynamics is obtained. The approach is applied to the fluidic pinball at Re=30, a canonical configuration of three identical circular cylinders arranged in an equilateral triangle and immersed in uniform flow under symmetric actuation. The model is validated against several representative actuation scenarios and accurately reproduces the transient dynamics without requiring unsteady training data, providing an interpretable, observable-based and control-oriented framework. The proposed description of actuated bluff-body flows is expected to be generalisable to other configurations.

infographic.key_insight: A feature-based reduced-order manifold can replace POD modes to model transient bluff-body wakes under arbitrary time-varying actuation with an interpretable analytical dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a control-oriented surrogate for actuated wakes that can predict response without requiring unsteady training data, making it useful for flow control design.
method: Replace POD modes with a feature-based manifold of the same dimension.
Build the state space from dynamic features that encode coherent-structure evolution.
Augment the state with transient actuation-response terms to obtain simple analytical dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model is validated on the fluidic pinball at Re=30 across several representative actuation scenarios and is reported to accurately reproduce transient dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on a canonical low-Reynolds-number configuration, so generalization to more complex or higher-Re flows still needs careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Feature-based manifold model of actuated wakes

title: Entropy-Constrained Machine Learning with Residual Data Augmentation for Modeling Chemical Kinetics
authors: Okezzi Ukorigho, Opeoluwa Owoyele
abstract: We present a physics-constrained machine learning framework for accelerating the direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent reacting flows. The model replaces the direct evaluation of detailed chemical source terms with a surrogate that predicts reaction rates from a reduced thermochemical state. To improve physical consistency, the second law of thermodynamics is incorporated as a training constraint by enforcing non-negative entropy generation, which restricts the evolution of the thermochemical state to physically admissible directions and improves stability during time integration. The approach is demonstrated on DNS of a two-dimensional planar lean premixed methane-air flame interacting with a turbulent flow field. The model reproduces detailed-chemistry results with high fidelity while achieving more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. Furthermore, a residual-based synthetic data augmentation strategy enables parametric exploration by constructing new training data from the original dataset, allowing accurate simulation at new inlet conditions without additional detailed-chemistry CFD runs. These results demonstrate that thermodynamically constrained machine learning can provide reliable and computationally efficient surrogates for detailed chemistry in high-fidelity combustion simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A thermodynamically constrained surrogate can replace expensive detailed chemistry in reacting-flow DNS while preserving physically admissible evolution and stable time integration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables high-fidelity combustion simulation at a fraction of the cost, with accurate transfer to new inlet conditions using synthetic residual-based augmentation.
method: Train a machine-learning surrogate to predict chemical source terms from a reduced thermochemical state.
Enforce non-negative entropy generation during training to satisfy the second law and constrain state evolution.
Use residual-based synthetic data augmentation to expand the training set for parametric generalization without new DNS runs.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 2D planar lean premixed methane-air flame DNS, the surrogate matched detailed-chemistry results closely and reduced computational cost by more than an order of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Entropy constraints improve physical consistency, but performance may depend on how well the reduced state and synthetic augmentation cover conditions outside the original training regime.
infographic.paper_title: Entropy-Constrained Machine Learning with Residual Data Augmentation for Modeling Chemical Kinetics

title: Developing Machine Learning Models of Subgrid Turbulent Transport for Quiet Sun 3D Radiative Hydrodynamic Simulations
authors: Rimsha Hameed Syeda, Dustin Kempton, Viacheslav Sadykov, Irina Kitiashvili, Rafal Angryk
abstract: Numerical modeling of solar plasma dynamics is affected by the resolution of the computational grid. This often requires the estimation of subgrid processes related to the small-scale flow turbulence, as these processes play a critical role in momentum transport and energy dissipation. In this work, we investigate the use of deep learning techniques as surrogate models for subgrid turbulent transport in realistic hydrodynamic simulations of the quiet Sun. We describe the development of a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to capture spatial dependencies in 3D velocity fields, leveraging different activation functions, as well as different architectural designs. We specifically focus on the prediction of Reynolds stress tensor components. The resultant model integrates velocity vector components and scalar features, such as plasma density, to enhance prediction accuracy. We compare the 3DCNN model to other types of models, such as a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) and physics-based Gradient and Smagorinsky models, and show that the final model design reconstructs the Reynolds stress tensor components more accurately. Specifically, a 3DCNN model achieves an average improvement of ~31% on diagonal components and ~8% on the off-diagonal components of the stress tensor. Additionally, we show that applying a logarithmic data transformation of the target stress tensor components, to handle heavily skewed data, improves model performance. Results demonstrate the potential of deep learning, particularly CNNs, to approximate Reynolds stress tensor components for the upper solar convection zone and lower atmosphere, making them a viable candidate for modeling subgrid processes and a promising alternative to traditional turbulence models.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D CNN using velocity, density, and log-transformed targets can better learn subgrid Reynolds stress transport in quiet-Sun radiative hydrodynamic simulations than MLP and classical turbulence closures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a data-driven surrogate for unresolved turbulent momentum transport and energy dissipation, which can improve reduced-order modeling in solar convection and atmosphere simulations.
method: Trained a 3D convolutional neural network on 3D velocity fields to predict Reynolds stress tensor components.
Included scalar plasma density alongside vector velocity components to improve spatially aware turbulence prediction.
Compared against an MLP and physics-based Gradient/Smagorinsky models, with log-transformed targets to reduce skewness effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The final 3DCNN improved average reconstruction by about 31% on diagonal stress components and about 8% on off-diagonal components versus baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on quiet-Sun simulation data, so generalization to other solar conditions, resolutions, or numerical setups still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Developing Machine Learning Models of Subgrid Turbulent Transport for Quiet Sun 3D Radiative Hydrodynamic Simulations
